source_text:
CAPUT QUARTUM.
De sacrae Scripturae affectionibus,
& quidem nominatim de
ejus AUTHORITATE.

I. Affectiones sacrae Scripturae sunt proprie illius qualitates, quibus divinitas ejus sufficienter declaratur, utpote authoritas, perfectio, claritas, sensus & interpretatio, efficacia.

II. Autoritas ejus est dignitas, qua omnium enunciationum suarum, propter Deum authorem, fidem meretur.

Est enim αὐτόπιστος, authentica, infallibilis, per omnia consentiens & immota fidei vitaeque nostrae regula divinitus constituta, 2. Tim. 3.16. Hinc recte Augustinus l.11. de civit. Dei cap. 3.: Titubabit fides, si divinarum scripturarum vacillet authoritas.
english:
CHAPTER FOUR
On the affections of Sacred Scripture, and specifically on its AUTHORITY

I. By affections of Sacred Scripture we mean the properties that belong to it properly speaking — the qualities that declare its divinity enough: authority, perfection, clarity, sense together with interpretation, and efficacy.

II. Authority here means that dignity on account of which, God being Author, every statement Scripture makes deserves to be believed. Scripture is self-attesting (αὐτόπιστος), authentic, and infallible; it agrees throughout and stands as the unmoved, God-appointed rule of our faith and life ([[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]). Augustine puts it rightly (City of God 11.3): if the divine Scriptures lose their authority, faith itself will stumble.

source_text: Ex his duabus postremis conclusionibus anamphibetōs perspicue more eorum quae oculis cernuntur deprehenditur primo, nos neque malitiosos et contentiosos, neque haereticos et apostatas esse aut videri posse, quia non solum nemini privatas opiniones, inventiones et imaginationes nostras obtrudere, verum etiam in caeteris, ad declinandum omnes noxias et non necessarias lites, cum Christianis aliis qui in fundamento nobiscum consentiunt, quantum per conscientiam licet, in ipsorum dogmatis sive placitis nos conformare cupimus. Neque aversamur aut vitamus quenquam praeter contentiosos et novos prophetas, qui verba hominum urgent et dicunt DOMINUS DIXIT (Jer. 23.21), quia ajunt: Hoc est Dei verbum, hoc est fidei articulus, quem si neges haereticus es — neque tamen has assertiones suas iis testimoniis adstruere possunt quibus prophetae et Apostoli conciones suas firmarunt; sed efficiunt ut praecepta Dei quae certa sunt negligantur (Jer. 23.30.32). Deinde, quantum ad opiniones quas hic innuimus, quoniam ea quae in Dei verbo tam clare perspicueque scripta sunt ut de illorum veritate nemo sanus et pacis amans justaeque aetatis Christianus jure dubitare possit, omnes pios quibus salus animarum suarum chara est monemus ut ab omnibus aliis parapleromasin sumentis seu additionibus sibi caveant quam studiosissime. 1. Quia hae tales additae controversae opiniones, si non falsae, saltem incertae ac dubiae sunt: unde periculum sit ne in superstitionem, idololatriam, imo spiritualem et abominabilem superbiam incidamus. 2. Quia, si fingamus has tales controversas opiniones neque falsas neque dubias sed veras ac certas esse, manet hoc saltem non necessarias esse, non solum quia non ab omnibus Christianis sciri, sed etiam quia neque omnes Christianos eas necessario concedere et amplecti oporteat, posteaquam illis rationes quibus niti videntur in scripturis ostensae fuerint — propterea quod non ita clare et evidenter in scripturis comprehensae sint ut adhibita omni debita diligentia mediisque hermeneuticis a timida ac pia conscientia, intuitu periculi jam modo indicati, cum laude aut saltem non injuria ab iis sibi temperare possit. 3. Quia periculum est saltem hac occasione multos pios et innocentes, qui metu conscientiae et consideratione ejus quod homo etiam cujusque otiosi verbi rationem reddere debeat in ultimo judicio (Matth. 12.36), controversas illas opiniones vitant et pro verbo Dei et articulis fidei habere nequeunt, injuria superbe judicari et condemnari, contra illud Servatoris (Matth. 7.1; Luc. 6.37) et Apostoli (Rom. 14.10.13; Gal. 6.2; 1 Cor. 8.2). Vide conciones Irenicas, cum appendice et Apologia ad D. Nicolaum Hunnium, editas a Cl. viro D. Conrado Bergio, collega meo et compatre charissimo, ubi hanc rem pie et erudite edisserit.
english: From these two last conclusions it is grasped beyond dispute, as plainly as things seen with the eyes, first that we neither are nor can seem malicious and contentious, nor heretics and apostates: because we desire not only to force on no one our private opinions, inventions, and imaginations, but also in other matters, to avoid all harmful and unnecessary quarrels, to conform ourselves — so far as conscience allows — to the dogmas or opinions of other Christians who agree with us in the foundation.

Nor do we turn from or avoid anyone except the contentious and new prophets who press men's words and say "THE LORD HAS SAID" ([[Jeremiah 23:21 >> Bible:Jeremiah 23:21]]), because they declare: "This is God's Word; this is an article of faith; if you deny it you are a heretic" — and yet cannot prop up these assertions with those testimonies by which the prophets and Apostles confirmed their sermons; but they bring it about that God's commandments, which are certain, are neglected ([[Jeremiah 23:30 >> Bible:Jeremiah 23:30]], [[Jeremiah 23:32 >> Bible:Jeremiah 23:32]]).

Next, as to the opinions we hint at here: since the things written so clearly and plainly in God's Word that no sound Christian who loves peace and is of ripe age can lawfully doubt their truth, we warn all the pious to whom their souls' salvation is dear to guard themselves as carefully as possible from all other fillings-out or additions. (1) Because such added controversial opinions, if not false, are at least uncertain and doubtful: whence there is danger of falling into superstition, idolatry, even spiritual and abominable pride. (2) Because even if we imagine such controversial opinions neither false nor doubtful but true and certain, this at least remains: they are not necessary — not only because not all Christians need know them, but also because not all Christians need necessarily grant and embrace them after the reasons they seem to rest on have been shown them in the Scriptures — since they are not so clearly and evidently comprehended in the Scriptures that a timid and pious conscience, using all due diligence and hermeneutical means, in view of the danger just indicated, cannot with praise or at least without wrong abstain from them. (3) Because there is at least this danger: that on this occasion many pious and innocent people who, from fear of conscience and from considering that a person must give account even of every idle word in the last judgment ([[Matthew 12:36 >> Bible:Matthew 12:36]]), avoid those controversial opinions and cannot hold them as God's Word and articles of faith, are unjustly and proudly judged and condemned — against the Savior's word ([[Matthew 7:1 >> Bible:Matthew 7:1]]; [[Luke 6:37 >> Bible:Luke 6:37]]) and the Apostle's ([[Romans 14:10 >> Bible:Romans 14:10]], [[Romans 14:13 >> Bible:Romans 14:13]]; [[Galatians 6:2 >> Bible:Galatians 6:2]]; [[1 Corinthians 8:2 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 8:2]]). See the Irenic sermons, with appendix and Apology to D. Nicolaus Hunnius, published by the distinguished D. Conrad Bergius, my colleague and dearest fellow-countryman, where he treats this matter piously and learnedly.

source_text:
Probationes humanae persuasionem humanam gignunt, fide Christiana infirmiorem, nisi divinum argumentum a sacris literis accedat.

XIV. Sequitur argumentum divinum: Spiritus sancti efficacia sacrae Scripturae indita… 1. Christiani malunt mori quam veritatem negare. 2. Assensus ab ipsa scriptura αὐτοπίστῳ (1. Thess. 2.13).
english: Proceed against atheists this way. Yet these proofs mostly rest only on human authority and produce only human persuasion — far weaker than Christian faith, unable to persevere in serious contest unless the divine argument from the sacred letters is added (Bellarmine, Bullinger, Valencia, Ficino, Mornay, Grotius).

XIV. So much for human arguments. Next the divine argument: the Holy Spirit's efficacy implanted in Sacred Scripture, by which its persuasive power is raised and breathed into the reader's heart — for which Christians receive it in the spiritual struggle with firm, unmoved, world-conquering, utterly divine assent.

1. Christians who watch for their soul's salvation assent so firmly that they would rather die than deny Scripture's divine truth. 2. This assent depends proximately on nothing else than Scripture itself as self-attesting (αὐτόπιστος), as [[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]] shows: they received the word not as a human word but as the word of God.

source_text: Testimonium divinum ab efficacia indita & interiore Spiritus operatione (arrhabo, σφραγίς, Esa. 4.4, Matth. 3.11). Contra Vitum Miletum Gamundianum, qui scripturam sine Ecclesiae authoritate Aesopi fabulis aequiparat.
english: This divine testimony is both from the efficacy so divinely implanted in Scripture that its authority does not of itself depend on proofs sought elsewhere, and from the Holy Spirit's inward operation in the reader's heart. That operation, though it cannot alone convince others, vehemently confirms the one who already reads and believes — called the earnest and seal given to believers, the spirit of judgment and of burning ([[Isaiah 4:4 >> Bible:Isaiah 4:4]]), and fire ([[Matthew 3:11 >> Bible:Matthew 3:11]]).

Those who by Aph. VII's monitory and motive arguments have already acknowledged the Christian religion as more probable cannot but admit this testimony's divinity. Therefore Vitus Miletus of Gmünd, a papal man, acts the atheist, not the Christian who knows Scripture's force, when he says: take away the Church's authority and Sacred Scripture will not even be worth Aesop's fables — take away the Church's infallible authority and tradition, and Scripture will have no certainty among humans.

source_text: CONCLUSIO III. Si quod dogma in scripturis non ita clare et evidenter invenitur ut ei contradici nequeat, legatur, et saltem incertum dubiumque sit an ab omnibus sanctis, quorum monumenta ad nos pervenerunt, unanimi consensu e scripturis deductum, creditum traditumque sit: fatemur nos hodie nullam causam videre ob quam id tanquam infallibile indubitatumque Dei verbum necessario credendum sit — imo cur non hic aut ille de eo dubitare possit. Nam quoniam prophetae omnes Mosen secuti, imo Apostoli et Christus ipse, siquid tanquam Dei verbum credendum tradiderunt quod non omnino manifestum et sine dubio ante scriptum fuerit, id tum e scriptura solidis consequentiis et legitimis interpretationibus, tum e signis aliisque indubitatis testimoniis demonstra verunt, adeo ut Dominus affirmare ausit, nisi opera inter eos operatus fuisset quae nemo alius operatus est, peccatum non haberent (Joh. 15.24) — quanto minus aliis credendum quod scripturis non continetur, nisi id scripturis aut signis testimoniisque fide dignis demonstrare possint? maxime cum salus nostra nihilominus constare nobis possit, si modo dogmata duabus prioribus conclusionibus comprehensa animo recipiamus. Quapropter non immerito nobis metuendum est ne forte verbum Dei non necessariis additionibus corrumpamus (Prov. 30.6; 2 Cor. 2.17), aliud Evangelium praedicemus (Gal. 1.8), Deumque tentemus si novum jugum discipulis imponamus (Act. 15.10), illudque ut necessarium et anamphibeton citra dubium credendum obtrudamus quod non constanter, unanimiter et publice ex sacra scriptura in Ecclesia DEI omni tempore traditum sit — et nobis haud immerito objicitur illud Augustini adversus Donatistas: An vos soli sapitis? An vos soli clare videtis? An omnes alios stipites existimatis et caecos? Nullane ecclesia praeter vestram synagogulam oculos habuit aut mentem?
english: CONCLUSION III. If some dogma is not found in the Scriptures so clearly and evidently that it cannot be contradicted, and it is at least uncertain and doubtful whether it has been deduced from the Scriptures, believed, and handed down by the unanimous consent of all the saints whose monuments have reached us — we confess we today see no cause why it must necessarily be believed as the infallible and undoubted Word of God; indeed, why this or that person may not doubt it.

For since all the prophets who followed Moses — indeed the Apostles and Christ Himself — if they handed down anything to be believed as God's Word that was not already altogether plain and written without doubt, demonstrated it both from Scripture by solid consequences and legitimate interpretations and from signs and other undoubted testimonies, so that the Lord dared to affirm that if He had not done among them works which no other did, they would not have sin ([[John 15:24 >> Bible:John 15:24]]) — how much less ought others to be believed for what is not contained in the Scriptures, unless they can demonstrate it by the Scriptures or by signs and testimonies worthy of faith? Especially since our salvation can nevertheless stand for us if only we receive in mind the dogmas comprehended in the two prior conclusions.

Therefore we not undeservedly fear lest we corrupt God's Word by unnecessary additions ([[Proverbs 30:6 >> Bible:Proverbs 30:6]]; [[2 Corinthians 2:17 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 2:17]]), preach another Gospel ([[Galatians 1:8 >> Bible:Galatians 1:8]]), and tempt God if we lay a new yoke on the disciples ([[Acts 15:10 >> Bible:Acts 15:10]]), and force as necessary and beyond dispute what has not been constantly, unanimously, and publicly handed down from Sacred Scripture in God's Church in every age. And not undeservedly is Augustine's word against the Donatists objected to us: "Are you alone wise? Do you alone see clearly? Do you count all others stocks and blind? Has no church besides your little synagogue had eyes or mind?"

source_text: Nostri scripturam primum principium discursus theologici cum Christiano statuunt; cum atheo processus aph. 13. Walaeus tria genera: historica κριτήρια; perfection/divinity religionis tribus notis; signa divinitatis (miracula, materia, forma, effecta, adjuncta antiquitatis/durationis).
english: What then, Miletus? If we made this principle simply first against every adversary, your charge would have some color. But ours set Sacred Scripture only as the first principle of theological discourse with one who professes himself a Christian and admits both Testaments. Against an utter atheist — still empty of Christ's Spirit ([[John 14:17 >> Bible:John 14:17]]) — the process is Aph. XIII's.

Walaeus wisely reduces convincing such a one to three kinds: (1) historical notes and criteria (Arrian; Josephus against Apion) — far more evident in sacred history than in human writings; (2) the religion's perfection and divinity in the Testaments, by three infallible notes — true God alone worshipped, true way of reconciliation, true duties to God and neighbor; (3) certain divinity-signs — miracles; matter (creation, Trinity, Christ God-man, resurrection, judgment, Decalogue, prayer, prophecies, promises); form (simplicity with majesty); effects (cessation of oracles, conversion of nations); adjuncts of antiquity and duration against Satan's hatreds. From these the books' divinity becomes known to anyone who seriously reads them with a sincere mind eager for salvation.

source_text: Barbari Apostolorum non Ecclesiae authoritate (tunc incognita; circularis), nec praedicatorum (piscatores), sed luminosa virtute verbi crediderunt. Assensus solidus aliquando sine cognita Ecclesiae authoritate; ergo non ab ea ut a causa per se. Bellarminus: nulla persuasio cogit ad articulos supernaturales nisi mens divinitus adjuvetur.
english: What moved the "barbarians" the Apostles taught to prefer death to deserting the faith? Not the human arguments (they produce only human faith); not the Church's authority (then unknown to them — and if proved from Scripture, circular); not the preachers' authority (unarmed fishermen and obscure weavers). Therefore they believed moved by the luminous power and spiritual efficacy of the Word itself, handed down to us through Scripture.

No effect that depends of itself on a cause can exist without that cause. But solid assent to Scripture sometimes exists without the Church's known authority. Therefore this assent does not depend on the Church's authority as on a cause of itself — as history shows of those who believed from New Testament reading alone. Bellarmine himself confesses: no persuasion can compel belief in supernatural articles unless the mind is divinely helped — not even miracles entirely convince.

source_text: Sicut autem Mosen secuti sunt prophetae caeteri, ita Jesum Christum secuti sunt Apostoli, quibus testimonium perhibent: primo, sacrae literae; secundo, doctrina et opera Christi notoria inter Judaeos; tertio, miracula Apostolorum; quarto, nubes testium qui Christum a resurrectione viderunt; quinto, constantia martyrum in ipsa morte gaudentium et pro inimicis orantium; sexto, evidentissimum complementum praedictionis de conversione gentium; septimo, excidium Hierosolymae et rejectio Judaeorum toties a prophetis praedicta. Sed et hic altera quaestio breviter decidenda est: Unde et quomodo nos, qui Christum profitemur, verum ac genuinum verbum Dei, cui unice deferamus, certe et infallibiliter hodie dignoscere possimus ac debeamus? Respondetur: 1. Nos, qui a primis Christianis et patribus spiritualis Israelis successimus, septimum testimonium adhuc oculis nostris usurpamus, quo scil. pacto Deus in Judaeis contemptum Evangelii sui ultus sit. 2. Experimur etiam sextum, vocationem gentium a DEO in nobis ipsis impleri. 3. Manifestum etiam est quintum, constantia eorum qui in adversis gaudent, pro inimicis orant, et omnia quam Christum perdere malunt. 4. Secundum, tertium et quartum — opera Christi et Apostolorum et vivi testes — non equidem oculis nostris usurpantur; attamen sicut olim Israeli secundum carnem constans, concors et publicum testimonium patrum tam certum erat ac si oculis suis vidissent, ita et nobis perpetuum, concors et publicum testimonium novi Israelis (omnium qui doctrinam Christi et Apostolorum profitentur) tam certum est, ac si ipsi exploravissemus. Ita et nobis testimonium omnium Christianorum, imo et Judaeorum quantum ad Vetus Testamentum, esse debet pro autopsiā qua uti potuissemus si illorum tempestate nobis vivere contigisset — cujus testimonii beneficio tam certi sumus de veritate Evangelii, quam certo ex historiis scimus Constantinopolin et Hierosolymam esse aut fuisse, etiamsi neutram ipsi unquam viderimus. Qui hoc testimonium vocat in dubium, multo potiore jure dubitabit de omnibus quae veteres Persae, Graeci, Romani et alii historici unanimi consensu scribunt ac testantur; nihilque aliud credet quam quod ipse vidit et manibus contraxit. 5. Durat etiamnum apud nos primum quoque testimonium, nempe scriptura prophetarum Veteris Testamenti, quae a Christo et Apostolis laudatur. Quibus testimoniis omnibus doctrina et scriptura Apostolorum, de qua nunquam dubitatum fuit a sanctis Dei, ab Apostolis profectam esse ita confirmatur, ut nemo sine notabili malitia et contumacia ejus divinam authoritatem ac veritatem hodie negare possit. Tertia quaestio superest de hodierno tempore, quo multi doctores et legati se nobis ingerunt et verbum Dei jactitant: Quodnam verum et infallibile Dei verbum sit? quid de dogmatibus sive opinionibus quae a Christianis aliquibus hodie foventur nobis statuendum sit? Haec quatuor conclusionibus determinatur, ut manifestum fiat in qua parte culpa schismatis potissimum haereat.
english: XV (continued). Just as the other prophets followed Moses, so the Apostles followed Jesus Christ. Testimony is given them: first, the sacred letters ([[Acts 17:2 >> Bible:Acts 17:2]]; [[Acts 18:24 >> Bible:Acts 18:24]]-[[Acts 18:28 >> Bible:Acts 18:28]]); second, Christ's doctrine and works then notorious among the Jews ([[Acts 2:22 >> Bible:Acts 2:22]]); third, the Apostles' miracles ([[Acts 2:43 >> Bible:Acts 2:43]]; [[Acts 5:12 >> Bible:Acts 5:12]]; [[Mark 16:20 >> Bible:Mark 16:20]]); fourth, the cloud of witnesses who saw Christ after His resurrection ([[1 Corinthians 15:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:6]]); fifth, the martyrs' constancy, rejoicing in death itself and praying for enemies ([[Acts 7:60 >> Bible:Acts 7:60]]; [[Hebrews 11:36 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:36]]; [[Hebrews 12:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 12:1]]); sixth, the clearest fulfillment of the oft-repeated prophecy of the nations' conversion to Israel's God ([[Romans 15:9 >> Bible:Romans 15:9]] and following); seventh, Jerusalem's ruin and the Jews' rejection so often foretold by the prophets.
But another question must be briefly decided here: From where and how can and ought we who confess Christ today know surely and infallibly the true and genuine Word of God, to which alone we defer?

The answer: (1) We who have succeeded the first Christians and the fathers of spiritual Israel still use with our own eyes the seventh testimony — how God has punished the Jews' contempt of His Gospel. (2) We also experience the sixth: the calling of the nations by God fulfilled in ourselves. (3) The fifth is likewise plain: the constancy of those who rejoice in adversity, pray for enemies, and would rather lose all than Christ. (4) The second, third, and fourth — Christ's and the Apostles' works, and the living witnesses who spoke with Christ after His resurrection — are not indeed seized by our eyes, nor do we see the Apostles annotate this or that with their own hand. Yet just as once for Israel according to the flesh the fathers' constant, concordant, and public testimony (whether of saints or not) was as certain as if they had seen with their eyes and heard with their ears, so for us the perpetual, concordant, and public testimony of the new Israel — of all who confess Christ's and the Apostles' doctrine — is as certain as if we ourselves had explored with eyes and ears what they unanimously attest. And as for ancient Israelites that fathers' testimony stood in place of the autopsy by which the fathers themselves had known, so for us the testimony of all Christians — and even of Jews as to the Old Testament — ought to stand in place of autopsy we could have used had we lived in their age. By that testimony's benefit we are as sure of the Gospel's truth as we surely know from histories that Constantinople and Jerusalem are or were, even if we never saw either. Whoever calls this testimony into doubt will with far better right doubt everything that ancient Persians, Greeks, Romans, and other historians write and attest by unanimous consent, and will believe nothing but what he himself has seen and handled with his hands. (5) The first testimony also still endures among us: the prophets' Scripture of the Old Testament, which Christ and the Apostles praise.

By all these testimonies the Apostles' doctrine and Scripture — never doubted by God's saints — is so confirmed to have come from the Apostles that no one without notable malice and obstinacy can today deny its divine authority and truth.

A third question remains about the present time, when many teachers and legates thrust themselves upon us and boast the Word of God: Which is the true and infallible Word of God? What are we to hold concerning dogmas or opinions some Christians today foster? This is determined in four conclusions, so that it may become plain in which part the fault of schism chiefly sticks.

source_text: Et cap. 211.: Ipsae creaturae in nullo fundantur nisi in solo DEO immediate: ita ipsa Biblia in nullo fundantur nisi in sola DEI authoritate immediate… Sic Gregorius de Valentia: Authoritas scripturae divina prorsus ac proinde omnino infallibilis. Petrus a Soto: Scripturam sacram ostendimus a Spiritu sancto scriptam esse: non itaque dubitandum est, quin illi ecclesia sit subdita — quia Spiritus sanctus revelat & dat ecclesiae scripturam sacram, quare non potest non illi subdita esse.
english: Raymond continues (ch. 211): Creatures are founded in nothing except God alone immediately. So too the Bible is founded in nothing except God's authority alone immediately. The certainty of the holy Bible's truth arises infallibly from God's authority alone, because He speaks.

So Gregory of Valencia: Scripture's authority is utterly divine and therefore entirely infallible. Peter a Soto: We show sacred Scripture was written by the Holy Spirit; therefore it is not to be doubted that the Church is subject to it. The Holy Spirit reveals and gives sacred Scripture to the Church; therefore the Church cannot but be subject to it — witnessing and interpreting not as superior to Scripture, but as subject.

source_text: CONCLUSIO IV. Si quid in scripturis non perspicue invenitur, nec ex iis ab omnibus sanctis unanimi consensu traditur, attamen illis non aperte et indubitato adversatur ac contradicit, et a concilio seu congregatione eorum Christianorum qui in capitibus praemissis nobiscum faciunt decernitur, non tamen instar Evangelii aut articuli fidei de quo nemini dubitandum sit, sed simpliciter tanquam vera utilisque doctrina quae in Ecclesia aut schola tradi possit proponitur: agnoscimus nos obligatos ad non contradicendum illi contentiose, sed aut ad consentiendum maxime cum iis quibuscum vivimus (ac proinde etiam quantum in nobis est pacem cum illis sectari tenemur), aut, si forte scrupulum de eo in conscientiis nostris sentiremus, eum opportune et commode proponendum, ut, si in quaestione de articuli cujusdam simpliciter et in se spectati veritate non consentire possimus, saltem in quaestione de illius pondere ac necessitate consensum tueamur: quod nimirum, etsi non omnino creditu necessarius sit, tamen in Ecclesia et scholis utiliter tradi aut saltem tolerari possit. Quin imo, si quis quantum ad articulum simpliciter et per se nobiscum sentiret (verbi gratia quod libri Judithae, Tobiae etc. non a prophetis scripti, ac perinde canonicis non sint isotimoi) dissentiret vero a nobis in pondere illius ac necessitate (quod videlicet ex hac causa is qui seorsim sentit et diversum constanter credit non sit tanquam haereticus condemnandus): obstrictos nos agnoscimus ut faciamus cum hoc qui in necessitate nobiscum consentit — quod nimirum articuli hujus neque affirmatio neque negatio ad salutem necessaria judicanda sit — eum vero qui in articulo simpliciter spectato nobiscum facit, in necessitate vero dissentit, habeamus pro tyranno aut haeretico qui discipulis jugum non necessarium imponat.
english: CONCLUSION IV. If something is not found plainly in the Scriptures, nor handed down from them by all the saints' unanimous consent, yet does not openly and undoubtingly oppose and contradict them, and is decided by a council or congregation of those Christians who agree with us in the foregoing heads — not, however, as a Gospel or article of faith about which no one may doubt, but simply proposed as true and useful doctrine that may be taught in the Church or school — we acknowledge ourselves bound not to contradict it contentiously, but either to consent especially with those with whom we live (and therefore, so far as in us lies, we are also bound to pursue peace with them), or, if we happen to feel a scruple about it in our consciences, to propose that scruple seasonably and conveniently: so that if we cannot agree on the question of some article's truth simply and in itself, we may at least keep consent on the question of its weight and necessity — namely that although it is not altogether necessary to believe, it may still be usefully taught or at least tolerated in the Church and schools.

Moreover, if someone agreed with us on the article simply and in itself (for example, that the books of Judith, Tobit, and the like were not written by the prophets and accordingly are not of equal honor with the canonical) yet dissented from us on its weight and necessity (namely that for this cause the one who thinks apart and constantly believes otherwise is not to be condemned as a heretic): we acknowledge ourselves bound to side with the one who agrees with us on necessity — namely that neither affirmation nor denial of this article is to be judged necessary to salvation — and to regard as a tyrant or heretic the one who agrees with us on the article simply considered yet dissents on necessity, because he lays an unnecessary yoke on the disciples.

source_text:
X. Inclinationes ad credendum sunt argumenta, quibus infideles moventur… ut religionem Christianam credibilem… agnoscant; alias motivae dicuntur.

XI. Consideranda earum varietas & usus. Saepe occasio non tantum est loco occasionis, sed & argumenti… Religio quae miraculis confirmatur & pro qua homines mortem oppetunt non potest esse vana.
english: X. Inclinations toward believing are arguments by which unbelievers are moved to acknowledge the Christian religion as credible and, by human persuasion, more probable than all others. Elsewhere they are called motives.

XI. Their variety and use must be considered. Often an occasion is not only in the place of an occasion but also of an argument. So the Church, proposing the Scriptures, moves as an argument when I consider so many cultivated nations embracing them with one consent as divinely revealed. The same holds for miracles and martyrdoms: A religion confirmed by miracles, and for which people face death, cannot be empty.

source_text: Sola Christiana a falso/absurdo/novitate immunis; antiquitas cum hominibus (Gen. 1; Eusebius); duratio ad finem mundi per Aegyptum, Babylonem, Alexandrum, Antiochum, Romanos, eversionem politiae, imperatores, Julianum. Ergo sola Christiana vera, aut nulla vera — Q.E.D.
english: The major rests on two foundations: what cannot be absent from the true religion belongs to no pagan religion; those marks belong to the Christian alone. False, absurd, and shameful things can be shown of Greek, Persian, and Roman superstitions, not of the Christian. The true religion has such antiquity that it has been as long as humans have ([[Genesis 1 >> Bible:Genesis 1]]; Eusebius), and pagan gods' very birthdays are known while the Hebrew-Christian religion began with humankind.

It is certain the true religion will last to the world's end. Yet pagan superstitions have perished. Ours endures through Egyptian bondage, Babylonian captivity, Alexander's wars, Antiochus Epiphanes (Josephus Ant. 12.7), Rome before Daniel's period ([[Daniel 9 >> Bible:Daniel 9]]), the polity's overthrow, emperors' fury, and Julian's temple grant (Ammianus 23.17). We conclude our religion rests on God's providence from the world's founding — which can be shown of no other. Therefore the Christian religion alone is true, or there is no true religion in the world — which was to be demonstrated.

source_text:
VI. Persuadetur autem divinitas ejus argumentis humanis aut divinis.

VII. Humana argumenta sunt vel occasiones credendi, vel inclinationes ad credendum. Illa monitoria, haec motoria dici possunt.

VIII. Occasiones sunt conditiones & causae sine quibus non…

IX. Occasiones credendi sunt vel personae… vel res… B. Augustino… Ego non crederem Euangelio, nisi me Ecclesiae catholicae authoritas commoveret, vel potius COMMONERET… Constantino M.… IN HOC SIGNO VINCES… Hodie… authoritas parentum… 2. Tim. 3.15.
english: VI. Its divinity is persuaded by human or divine arguments.
VII. Human arguments are either occasions of believing, or inclinations toward believing. The former may be called monitory, the latter motory.
VIII. Occasions are conditions and sine-qua-non causes ordinarily required before someone is moved to assent.

IX. Occasions of believing are either persons (doctors, parents, equals) by whom the sacred letters are commended, or things (favorable or adverse, ordinary or miraculous) without which faith in the Scriptures would not be had — though faith as effect does not of itself depend on those occasions. For Augustine the occasion was the Church's authority (Against the Epistle of the Foundation 5): "I would not believe the Gospel unless the catholic Church's authority moved me" — or rather, as the old Amerbach folio reads, "reminded me" (commoneret). For Constantine, the cross in the air: IN HOC SIGNO VINCES. For most of us today, parents' authority, as with Timothy ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]).

source_text: XV. Argumentum divinum tria continet: 1. verbum ipsum; 2. signa & testimonia certa; 3. sensus & ratio. Exemplo Mosis & Aaronis (Exod. 4.30; Deut. 5.27). Signa efficacia apud αὐτόπτας & posteros. Prophetae Mosen secuti. Legatus legatorum est JESUS CHRISTUS (Deut. 18.15); Apostoli Christum secuti.
english: XV. The divine argument by which the Holy Spirit through His legates persuades humans that what they propose is infallibly God's Word — which all to whom it is sufficiently proposed must receive as God's Word, so that those who do not are condemned as unbelievers — contains three things: (1) the Word itself, which God or some legate in God's name has spoken; (2) certain signs and testimonies by which humans not wholly obstinate are persuaded this is from God; (3) eyes, ears, sense and reason, by which they can infallibly perceive that Word and those signs.

1. When God sent Moses and Aaron, He gave them the Word and signs, but had already given sense and intellect to His people ([[Exodus 4:30 >> Bible:Exodus 4:30]]; [[Exodus 19:9 >> Bible:Exodus 19:9]]). Therefore Israel gladly embraced Moses' word as divine ([[Deuteronomy 5:27 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 5:27]]).

2. Those signs were efficacious not only among eyewitnesses (αὐτόπται) but among posterity, who have fathers' history and tradition instead of autopsy ([[Psalm 44:2 >> Bible:Psalm 44:2]]; [[Psalm 78:2 >> Bible:Psalm 78:2]]; [[Deuteronomy 4:9 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 4:9]]-[[Deuteronomy 4:10 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 4:10]]).
3. Other prophets followed Moses with equal authority, agreeing with the sacred letters already complete and pressing that no new worship be received.

4. The legate of legates, Apostle and High Priest of our confession, is JESUS CHRIST, whom Moses foretold ([[Deuteronomy 18:15 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 18:15]]). Testimony: sacred letters ([[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]], [[John 5:46 >> Bible:John 5:46]]; [[Luke 24:46 >> Bible:Luke 24:46]]; [[Acts 10:43 >> Bible:Acts 10:43]]); John the Baptist ([[John 1:7 >> Bible:John 1:7]]); God's voice from heaven ([[Matthew 3:17 >> Bible:Matthew 3:17]]; [[Matthew 17:5 >> Bible:Matthew 17:5]]; [[2 Peter 1:16 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:16]]); miracles ([[John 5:36 >> Bible:John 5:36]]; [[John 10:25 >> Bible:John 10:25]]); resurrection ([[Romans 1:4 >> Bible:Romans 1:4]]); ascension ([[Luke 24:51 >> Bible:Luke 24:51]]; [[Acts 1:9 >> Bible:Acts 1:9]]). As prophets followed Moses, so the Apostles followed Christ.

source_text:
Contrariam opinionem Henricus Eckhardus nostris parum candide impingit fasciculi sui cap.1. q.2. detorquens verba Bezae… Et Piscatoris… Deum interdum verbo significare se velle, quod revera non vult; aut nolle, quod revera vult.

Quibus magnis viris occasionem ita loquendi praebuere verba Mosis Gen. 22.2.12., Exod. 9.1.12. & cap. 10.20. & 4.21. non ut vere contrarias voluntates Deo tribuant… Est duntaxat in verbis Mosis ἐναντιοφάνεια inde ortum, quod Deus per verbum quidem semper significet, se aliquid velle, quod vere vult; non tamen semper significet, se id praecise velle, quod nos eum velle prima fronte concipimus.
english: Henry Eckhardus unfairly foists a contrary opinion on our teachers (Fasciculus 1.q.2), twisting Beza's words and Piscator's — that God sometimes by the Word signifies He wills what He does not truly will, or refuses what He truly wills.

Those great men took occasion from Moses' words ([[Genesis 22:2 >> Bible:Genesis 22:2]], [[Genesis 22:12 >> Bible:Genesis 22:12]]; [[Exodus 9:1 >> Bible:Exodus 9:1]], [[Exodus 9:12 >> Bible:Exodus 9:12]]; [[Exodus 10:20 >> Bible:Exodus 10:20]]; [[Exodus 4:21 >> Bible:Exodus 4:21]]) — not to ascribe truly contrary wills to God. Far be it from our doctors to charge the Scriptures with that! There is only an apparent opposition (ἐναντιοφάνεια) in Moses' words: God always signifies by the Word that He wills something He truly wills; He does not always signify that He precisely wills what we first imagine Him to will. If Eckhardus wants to be a fair interpreter, let him learn candor.

source_text:
III. Eaque spectatur vel absolute in se ratione naturae suae, ut est, vel comparate ratione nostrae cognitionis.

IV. Absolute & in se ratione suae naturae, est divina, quia est a Deo.

Sic testatur Paulus 1. Thess. 2.v.13. 2. Tim. 3.v.16. 1. Pet. 1.21… Raimundus de Sabunde… Cum honor sit credere alicui in verbis ejus, sequitur quod homo debet credere DEO… sine alio testimonio… Si enim non volo credere verbis DEI propterea quia ipse dicit, sed quaero aliam probationem, tunc magis credo alicui alteri quam DEO.
english: III. That authority is viewed either absolutely in itself, by the reason of its own nature as it is, or comparatively, by the reason of our cognition.

IV. Absolutely and in itself, by the reason of its nature, it is divine, because it is from God. So Paul testifies ([[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[1 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:1 Peter 1:21]]). Raymond of Sabunde (Natural Theology ch. 209) writes truly: Since it is an honor to believe someone on his words, a human being ought to believe God — first of Himself, without another witness, purely on His bare word. If I refuse to believe God's words because He says them, and hunt another proof, then I trust someone else more than God.

source_text:
V. Comparate & ratione nostrae cognitionis, quatenus illius veritas homini sano & pietatis sensu praedito certis argumentis persuadetur.

Hic quaeritur, unde nobis constet sacram Scripturam esse θεόπνευστον & αὐτόπιστον? Determinandum tum adversus atheos (Celsus, Porphyrius, Julianus), tum adversus pontificios, qui auctoritatem ejus e Romanae ecclesiae testimonio suspendunt — ut Nicolaus Cusanus, Sylvester Prieras, Verratus, Eccius, Rutlandus, Viguerius, Hosius, Andradius, Bozius, Pighius, a Soto, Tapperus, Stapletonus, Salmeron, Gordonus Huntlaeus.
english: V. Comparatively, and by the reason of our cognition — insofar as its truth is persuaded to a sound person endowed with a sense of piety by certain arguments.

Here the question is: whence is it established that Sacred Scripture is θεόπνευστος and αὐτόπιστος — divinely inspired and of itself worthy of faith? That must be settled both against atheists who, with Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian, call Scripture's divinity into doubt, and against the papal party, who hang its authority on the testimony of their Roman Church — Cusa, Prierias, Verratus, Eck, Rutland ("no Scripture authentic without the Church's authority; therefore the Church's is greater"), Viguerius (Scripture to Church as body to soul), Hosius, Andradius, Bozius, Pighius, a Soto, Tapper, Stapleton, Salmeron, Gordon Huntly.

source_text: CONCLUSIO II. Si quod dogma forte in scripturis occurrat, quod non prorsus extra controversiam et aliorum contradictionem sit, attamen non modo multis scripturae testimoniis probabile fiat, verum etiam clare ac perspicue ab omnibus sanctis, quorum scripta ad nos pervenerunt, vi testimoniorum illorum ita traditum creditumque sit, ut etiam laicis quibus sana mens sit unanimem eorum consensum facile demonstrare possimus: de eo fatemur neminem pium et pacis amantem controversiam movere debere, sed monelam Apostoli potius sequi, 1 Cor. 1.10: Precor autem vos, fratres, per nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ut idem loquamini omnes, et non sint inter vos dissidia, sed sitis compacti eadem mente et eadem sententia. Phil. 2.2: Explete meum gaudium, ut idem sapiatis, eandem charitatem habentes, unanimes et sentientes unum. Sic nos a Photinianis separamus, qui quidem et ipsi nonnunquam praxin eorum quae clara et certa sunt urgere videntur; at interim certamina movent etiam de iis quae plurimis et certissimis scripturae testimoniis simplicissime intellectis definita sunt inde ab Ecclesiae incunabulis. Ex his duabus prioribus conclusionibus, quibus omnia cuique Christiano explicite scitu et creditu necessaria continentur, palam est nos neminem velle seducere, quia opiniones, inventiones, subtiles interpretationes et consequentias nostras nemini obtrudimus, sed hoc unice credendum commendamus quod e sacra scriptura semper a sanctis Dei publice et perspicue traditum est: certo statuentes neminem de salute sua periclitari posse qui in his dogmatis sese ex animo ac diligenter exerceat.
english: CONCLUSION II. If some dogma happens to occur in the Scriptures that is not wholly beyond controversy and others' contradiction, yet is not only made probable by many Scripture testimonies but also has been so clearly and plainly handed down and believed by all the saints whose writings have reached us, by the force of those testimonies, that even laypeople of sound mind can easily demonstrate their unanimous consent — concerning that we confess no pious lover of peace ought to raise controversy, but rather follow the Apostle's warning ([[1 Corinthians 1:10 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:10]]): "I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment." And ([[Philippians 2:2 >> Bible:Philippians 2:2]]): "Fulfill my joy, that you be like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind."

So we separate ourselves from the Photinians, who indeed sometimes seem to urge the practice of things that are clear and certain, yet meanwhile raise contests even about matters defined from the Church's cradle by very many and most certain Scripture testimonies understood in the simplest way.

From these two prior conclusions, which contain everything each Christian must explicitly know and believe, it is plain we wish to seduce no one: we force on no one our opinions, inventions, subtle interpretations, and consequences, but commend solely this as to be believed which has always been publicly and plainly handed down from Sacred Scripture by God's saints — settling for certain that no one can be in peril for his salvation who exercises himself in these dogmas from the heart and diligently.

source_text: Inspiciendae leges gentium & religiones (omnes absurdae praeter Christianam); populus Judaicus & Moses; Christiani in Mose fundati (Grotius, Justinus, Ficinus, Mornaeus). Aut religio Christiana, cujus sacra scriptura principium est, vera est religio, aut nulla est in orbe vera religio. Atqui falsum est nullam esse… Ergo Christiana vera.
english: First, inspect kingdoms' laws, whose only end is fleeting earthly good. Second, inspect all nations' religions: though they promise eternal life, none escapes being shown absurd from reason itself. Whatever right reason plainly teaches false is false also in theology — the same thing cannot be true and false at once.

Third, come to the Jewish people, whom even pagans acknowledge as most ancient, and whose Moses leaves Greek historical memory behind. Fourth, from Moses demonstrate how God revealed Himself and the way to eternal life. Fifth, prove that what Christians teach is founded in Moses — as Grotius, Justin Martyr, Ficino, and Mornay did. Sixth, argue: Either the Christian religion, whose principle is Sacred Scripture, is the true religion, or there is no true religion in the world. But it is false that there is none (from providence, nn. 5–6). Therefore the Christian religion is the true religion.

source_text: XIII. Usus argumentorum horum talium est proprie ad convincendum infideles & atheos. 1. Infidelis aut negat Deum… aut concedit. 2–3. Si negat, habitu philosophico… 4–7. Si concedit: vanitas suae religionis; Dei cura salutis; providentia terrena absque aeterna absurda; ergo doctrina divinitus revelata dari debet.
english: XIII. The use of such arguments is properly to convince unbelievers and atheists. Against true Christians who watch for their souls there is no need of them.

1. The unbeliever either denies that God is, that He is one, truthful, just and good, that the soul is immortal, and that there will be another life — or he grants these. 2. If he denies them, the theologian can do nothing in the theological habit. 3. Therefore convince him in the philosophical habit from nature's principles. 4. If he grants them, first show his religion's vanity. 5. Second, propose that God of infinite goodness takes greatest care of the human being — and that it would clash with that goodness never to reveal His will concerning salvation. 6. Politics makes it plain: providence is credited with kingdoms' preservation; it would be absurd to supply earthly life richly while neglecting eternal life for an immortal soul. 7. Third, once God's care for salvation is proved, some divinely revealed doctrine showing the way to eternal life must be given.

source_text: CONCLUSIO I. Omne id, quod indubitatis Veteris ac Novi Testamenti scriptis ita clare ac perspicue comprehensum est, ut a nemine sanae mentis in dubium vocari possit, necessario credendum et fatendum est. Hoc enim nititur omnibus testimoniis illis quae de prophetica et Apostolica doctrina citavimus. Ubi tamen cuivis intelligere in proclivi est, nos non solum nudam literam qua verbum Dei semel enunciatum fuit, verum etiam omnes e scriptura sumptas interpretationes, exhortationes et consequentias recipere oportere, quae ita affectae sunt ut in eas omnes Christianorum sectae, et cumprimis Papistae, Lutherani, Calviniani (ut vocantur), manifesto et unanimi consensu conspirent. Dogmatum vero extra omnem controversiam apud hos positorum tantus est numerus, tanta moles, ut, siquidem ea prius omnia seligere et ipso opere exprimere libeat — ne verbum Dei superficie oris duntaxat circumferamus, sed cordis centro recipiamus — propemodum nostra sponte obliviscamur tum superfluarum controversiarum, tum humanarum additionum, quae sunt sive illorum qui alios sine expresso Dei verbo condemnant et persequuntur, sive istorum qui sine diserto Dei verbo contra catholice receptos fidei articulos lites non necessarias movent.
english: CONCLUSION I. Everything so clearly and plainly comprehended in the undisputed writings of the Old and New Testament that no one of sound mind can call it into doubt must necessarily be believed and confessed. For this rests on all those testimonies we cited concerning prophetic and Apostolic doctrine.

Yet anyone can readily understand that we ought to receive not only the bare letter by which God's Word was once uttered, but also all interpretations, exhortations, and consequences drawn from Scripture that are so conditioned that all Christian parties — and especially those called Papists, Lutherans, and Calvinists — conspire into them by open and unanimous consent.

Indeed the number and mass of dogmas placed beyond all controversy among these is so great that if one first chooses to select them all and express them in deed — so that we do not merely carry God's Word about on the surface of the mouth but receive it in the heart's center — we almost spontaneously forget both superfluous controversies and human additions, whether of those who condemn and persecute others without God's express Word, or of those who without God's plain Word stir unnecessary quarrels against the catholically received articles of the faith.

limits: Sampling and structural checks do not prove whole-work fidelity or completeness.
